message.content: Nicolaus Copernicus developed his heliocentric theory during the early 16th century, a period of intense religious authority and political upheaval across Europe. The Catholic Church dominated intellectual life, and challenges to geocentrism carried serious theological risks. The Protestant Reformation was reshaping political boundaries, while the Holy Roman Empire struggled with internal divisions. His work, though brilliant, bore a cactiform structure of careful hedging to avoid immediate ecclesiastical condemnation. Copernicus, a canon in Frombork, lived where science and theology were inseparable, making his ideas extraordinary yet dangerous to present openly.
